summary: Updates how trustees of the IETF Trust are selected. Because the IAOC was eliminated, its members no longer double as trustees, so trustees are chosen separately. Everything else about the Trust is unchanged. It obsoletes RFC 4371.

plainLanguage.summary: The IETF Trust holds intellectual property on behalf of the IETF. Its five trustees used to be the members of a committee that no longer exists. This RFC sets out how the trustees are now chosen, and changes nothing else about the Trust.

questions: how many trustees does the ietf trust have
subtitle: Why the IETF Trust's five trustees are now picked on their own instead of coming from a defunct oversight committee.

tldr.problem: The trustees of the IETF Trust were also the members of the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee, and that committee has now been eliminated.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC replaces the old rule with a separate selection process: three trustees are appointed by the IETF Nominating Committee and confirmed by the IESG, one is appointed by the IESG, and one by the ISOC Board of Trustees.
tldr.outcome: Only the selection of trustees changes; every other aspect of the IETF Trust stays as it was. The RFC obsoletes RFC 4371 and asks the trustees to amend the Trust Agreement.

today: RFC 8714 is a Best Current Practice published in February 2020. It obsoleted RFC 4371 and has not been obsoleted since. It changes only how the trustees of the IETF Trust are selected; the rest of the Trust is unchanged.

sections.title: Why Trustee Selection Changes
sections.content:
The IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC) members used to act as trustees of the IETF Trust, so the same people both oversaw the administration of the IETF and held its intellectual property. The IAOC has been eliminated as part of an update to the structure of the IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA), and this memo specifies that the trustees are selected separately.

The memo obsoletes RFC 4371. The changes relate only to the selection of trustees; all other aspects of the IETF Trust remain as they are. Section 2 of the document copies the definition of the Trust as it was in RFC 4371, leaving out only the part about trustee selection and adding a reference to the IETF Trust website. The reasoning for the change, and the rationale for these particular changes, is in RFC 8715.
sections.plainLanguage: The same people used to run the IETF's administration and look after its intellectual property. One of those two jobs no longer exists, so the Trust's trustees are now picked separately. Nothing else about the Trust changes.

sections.title: What the IETF Trust Is
sections.content:
A Trust, the IETF Trust, has been formed for the purpose of acquiring, holding, maintaining and licensing certain existing and future intellectual property and other property used in connection with the administration of the IETF. The Trust was formed by the signatures of its Settlors and initial Trustees.

The Settlors, who contributed initial intellectual property to the Trust, were the Internet Society (ISOC) and the Corporation for National Research Initiatives. The Beneficiary of the IETF Trust is the IETF as a whole. Further details are on the IETF Trust's website.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF Trust holds property and intellectual property that belongs to the IETF as a whole. Two organisations, the Internet Society and the Corporation for National Research Initiatives, put the first of it into the Trust.

sections.title: How the Five Trustees Are Appointed
sections.content:
In the revised structure there will be five trustees. Three shall be appointed by the IETF Nominating Committee (NomCom) and confirmed by the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG). One shall be appointed by the IESG, and one shall be appointed by the Internet Society (ISOC) Board of Trustees. The appointments by the IESG and by the ISOC Board of Trustees do not require confirmation.

The IETF Trust Chair informs the nominating committee of the trustee positions to be reviewed, and the IETF Trust provides a summary of the expertise desired of the trustee candidates to each appointing body. The document revises the original trustee selection procedures of RFC 4071 and RFC 4371 to eliminate the requirement that trustees be drawn from the members of the IAOC.

A change to the Trust Agreement is required to put this change into effect. The document requests that the current trustees make this change at the earliest convenient time and no later than the end of the 104th IETF meeting in March 2019.
sections.plainLanguage: Five trustees sit on the Trust. Three are nominated by the IETF Nominating Committee and then confirmed by the IESG; one is appointed by the IESG and one by the Internet Society's board. The change needs a new Trust Agreement to take effect.

sections.title: Terms of Office and Staggering
sections.content:
The terms of the trustees appointed by the IETF Nominating Committee are three years. The initial selection is one, two and three year terms, in order to stagger the terms from the start. The appointments by the IESG and by the ISOC Board of Trustees are two-year terms, with the initial terms being one and two years respectively. The goal of the staggered initial terms is to minimise potential trustee turnover in any single year.

To maintain the stagger, each appointing body may, at its discretion, appoint trustees for shorter terms as needed in exceptional situations, for example for mid-term vacancies or when an appointment is not ready by the time of the first IETF meeting of the year.
sections.plainLanguage: Nominated trustees serve three years and the other two serve two. The first appointments are shorter and out of step with each other, so that no year sees a large number of trustees leave at once.

sections.title: The Chair, Recall and Turnover
sections.content:
Once the initial trustee selections according to this document are complete, and at each subsequent annual meeting of the IETF Trust once new trustees are seated, the trustees shall elect one trustee to serve as IETF Trust Chair by a majority vote of the IETF Trust.

Trustees appointed by the IETF Nominating Committee may be recalled according to the recall process described in BCP 10. Trustees appointed by the IESG or by the ISOC Board of Directors may be recalled by the appointing body. For appointments made by the IESG, the IESG is expected to run an open selection process and to consider the necessary skill set and conflicts of interest as part of that process.
sections.plainLanguage: The trustees pick one of their number to chair the Trust, by a vote. Nominated trustees can be recalled under the process in BCP 10; the other two are recalled by whoever appointed them.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that this memo has no security implications for the Internet, and that the document has no IANA actions. The whole document concerns who sits on the IETF Trust; nothing in it changes how a protocol or any data is handled, and it registers no names, numbers or protocol parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The document has no effect on the security of the Internet and asks for no registrations. It is a set of rules about people and appointments.

Terms, chair and recall in the revised structure

items.title: Staggered starts
items.text: The first terms are one, two and three years for the nominated trustees, and one and two years for the other two, to reduce turnover in any single year.

items.title: Shorter terms in exceptions
items.text: An appointing body may shorten a term for a mid-term vacancy or when an appointment is not ready by the first IETF meeting of the year.

items.title: A chair from among the trustees
items.text: Once new trustees are seated, the trustees elect one of their number as IETF Trust Chair by majority vote.

items.title: Recall
items.text: Nominated trustees may be recalled under BCP 10; trustees appointed by the IESG or the ISOC board are recalled by the appointing body.
